# Versioning model: git-versioned snapshots vs. an append-only event log

Two ways to version this catalog's metadata:

**A (what this repo does)**: `.cue` schema + `.json` data, hand-edited or mechanically regenerated by
`scripts/rebuild_*.py`, versioned as full-file snapshots in git. History = a sequence of commits, each a
complete replacement of the data files. Consumers pin to a commit/tag; `check_semver.py` diffs two tags.

**B (the alternative)**: every individual change (a field flips, a volume appears, a status changes)
becomes one immutable, timestamped, append-only log entry. No git. Current state = fold/replay all entries
up to "now"; state as of any past instant = fold/replay up to that timestamp. This is the same shape as
the `Human`/`LogEntry`/`AppendLog` design discussed earlier this session for raw zarr snapshot management,
just applied to the metadata catalog instead of the pixel data.

## The load-bearing difference: where does the source of truth actually live?

This is the question that decides most of the rest. For **B** to be worth building, the log itself needs
to be authoritative — the kind of system event sourcing is built for is one where there's no external
ground truth to fall back on, so the log *is* the only record of what happened.

That's not this catalog. The real ground truth for `volumes` is a directory walk of `#DataRoot`; the real
ground truth for `annotations` is the `mia_annotation` GitHub Project. Both are already, independently,
mechanically re-derivable from outside this repo — that's the entire point of `rebuild_volumes.py`/
`rebuild_annotations.py`. A catalog built this way doesn't need a trustworthy history of every past change
to reconstruct current truth; it needs a trustworthy way to re-ask the external source of truth, which it
already has. This shows up concretely: when the corpus grew from 417 to 838 volumes, nothing needed to
replay 421 append events — a single fresh `rebuild_volumes.py` run produced the correct new state,
verified as byte-identical to the old 417 plus purely additive new entries. An append-only log adds real
value when there's no re-derivation path and the log is the only witness; here there always is one.

## What git-versioned snapshots (A) get for free

- **Diffing, blame, tagging, branching** — already fully built, battle-tested, and every collaborator
  already knows it. `check_semver.py` leans on `git show <ref>:<file>` directly; building the equivalent
  "diff state as of two points" for a bespoke log format is buildable (fold to each point, diff the two
  folds) but is now something *we'd* own and test, not something git already solved.
- **Self-correcting wholesale rebuilds** — a `rebuild_*.py` run replaces the entire file with a fresh
  derivation from ground truth, so any historical mistake (a bad hand-edit, an old rebuild script's bug)
  is corrected on the next run without needing to locate and fix or compensate a specific past log entry.
- **An established editing mental model** — hand-edit a text file, review the diff, commit. An append-only
  log can't be "corrected" the normal way once a wrong entry lands (the discipline requires appending a
  compensating entry, never editing) — for a collaborator base of ML/imaging scientists rather than
  infra/systems people, that's a meaningfully higher-friction mental model for what should be routine.
- **Space/compaction handled by git** — git's packing already avoids storing near-duplicate full snapshots
  wastefully. A hand-rolled append-only log of individually-timestamped field changes would eventually
  need its own periodic-snapshot/compaction strategy to keep replay fast — which is, again, re-deriving
  something close to "git commits" from scratch.

## What an append-only log (B) would get that snapshots lose

- **True per-change timestamps, not per-commit-batch timestamps.** When `rebuild_annotations.py` pulled 15
  legitimate GitHub updates in one run, they landed as one commit with one timestamp — you can't tell from
  git history alone which of those 15 field changes happened first in the real world, only that all 15
  were *noticed* at the same time. A log sourced directly from GitHub's own event timestamps wouldn't lose
  that ordering.
- **Natural "state as of an arbitrary instant" queries.** Git's "state as of time T" means "state as of
  whichever commit was current at T" — accurate only to commit granularity, and commits land whenever
  someone happens to run a rebuild, not when the real-world change happened. A log queried by timestamp
  answers this exactly, not approximately.
- **Conflict-free by construction.** Appending is commutative; two people (or two automated jobs) adding
  entries concurrently merge trivially, where two people editing the same JSON snapshot concurrently can
  produce a real git merge conflict. Low-probability here (few people run the rebuild scripts), but not
  zero.

## A realization this comparison surfaces: for annotations, the log already exists — upstream

GitHub already retains full history of every field/status change on a Project item, via its own timeline/
audit trail. `rebuild_annotations.py` currently only ever calls `gh project item-list`, which returns the
*current* snapshot — every prior state of issue #12 (before its `bbox`/`tool`/`status` were filled in,
observed directly this session as a live diff) is discarded the moment we overwrite `lmd_annotations.json`
with the new pull. If point-in-time reconstruction of annotation state ever becomes a real requirement
(e.g. "what did the corpus's annotation status look like as of the date a given model was trained"),
building our own append-only log would be redundant work — the more accurate source is GitHub's own
history, which this catalog doesn't currently query at all. Worth remembering before ever building a
parallel logging system for data that already has an upstream one.

## Addendum: why not cut GitHub out entirely and hand-edit the annotations data in this repo?

Worth asking directly, since the previous section already shows GitHub's history is more authoritative
than anything we'd build ourselves: is there anything in `#AnnotationItem` that's actually derived, or is
it all just hand-typed somewhere anyway — in which case, why not hand-type it here instead?

Checked field by field. `roi` is the one real exception (computed by `rebuild_annotations.py` from
`bbox`/`bbox_size`). Every other field — `status`, `dataset`, `tool`, `task`, `model_organism`,
`data_modality`, `structure_of_interest`, `priority`, `annotator`, `assignees`, `completion_pct`,
`label_count`, `timepoint`, `bbox`/`bbox_size` themselves, `fileglancer_path`, `gt_export_path`,
`gt_ingested_path`, `proofread_*_path`, `wk_link`, `wk_ann_link`, `source_paths` — is hand-typed by a human
somewhere, currently in GitHub Project fields, with no technical reason it couldn't be hand-typed directly
into this repo's JSON/CUE instead.

So the "is it derived" test alone doesn't settle it — the deciding factor is who's doing the typing and
what they're using it for, not whether a machine could technically replace GitHub as the storage location:

- **Different audience.** The people filling these fields in — annotators named directly in this data
  (Diana Ramirez, Alannah Post, Brie Yarbrough, Cat Mori, Tiffany Tran, Carla Rodriguez, and others) — work
  in WebKnossos/Amira/Paintera, not git. GitHub's Project board gives them a Kanban UI, dropdowns, and text
  fields with zero technical skill required. Hand-editing CUE/JSON and using git instead puts the wrong
  tool in front of the wrong audience — the realistic outcome is worse data quality (typos, broken syntax,
  blocked commits), not better.
- **Concurrency.** Multiple annotators update different issues throughout the day, sometimes the same
  issue. GitHub Projects is a real multi-tenant database under its UI — concurrent edits are atomic, no
  merge-conflict concept exists. A git-versioned JSON file hand-edited by a dozen non-technical people
  would get real conflicts and silently-lost updates (a stale local copy clobbering a more recent edit),
  since none of them would practice careful git discipline.
- **It's the source of the fine-grained audit trail the previous section already leans on.** If annotators
  hand-edited a shared JSON file instead of using GitHub's UI, the realistic pattern is large batched
  commits ("updated a bunch of stuff today") replacing the timestamped, per-field history GitHub already
  provides automatically — undermining the exact property just argued for above.
- **It's the same boundary question as the miao-config discussion (`schema.md`/earlier session), mirrored.**
  "Fully specifying a miao config belongs in the model repo that owns it, not upstream in this catalog" —
  the same logic applies in reverse here: annotation *workflow* (who's assigned, what stage a crop is at,
  discussion about it) belongs where the annotators actually work, not hijacked into a downstream,
  consumer-facing catalog repo. This repo and the GitHub Project serve genuinely different audiences (ML
  engineers pinning stable data vs. annotators managing daily work); merging them compromises both instead
  of simplifying either.

What cutting GitHub out would actually buy is narrower than it first looks: no more `FIELD_MAP`
casing guesswork (`data_Modality`, `wK_Ann_Link`), no `read:project` scope friction, and no
`PENDING_UPSTREAM_FIXES` staleness risk. Real, but it's a complaint about *this repo's integration code*
(a one-time cost, already paid and documented), not evidence that GitHub Projects is the wrong tool for
annotators day-to-day. `rebuild_annotations.py` exists precisely so both sides keep the tool suited to
them — annotators keep GitHub, consumers keep a stable, versioned, machine-checked JSON — rather than
forcing one group to live with the other's interface.

## A gap this comparison surfaces: for volumes, we're discarding a real timestamp we already have for free

Filesystem `.zarr` directories carry real creation/modification times (`ctime`/`mtime`) that
`rebuild_volumes.py` doesn't read or record at all — the only timestamp attached to "when did this volume
appear" today is whenever someone happened to next run the rebuild script and commit it (we saw this
directly: the NernLab volume/annotation pair existed on GitHub for at least 2 days, `last_updated:
"2026-08-27"`, before this catalog noticed it). An append-only design would naturally want to capture the
real filesystem timestamp per volume; the current snapshot design has no field for it at all and silently
throws the information away on every rebuild. This is a real, cheap improvement independent of the
git-vs-log question — `rebuild_volumes.py` could start recording `os.stat(path).st_ctime` per volume today
without adopting event sourcing to get it.

## Failure modes, honestly, on both sides

- **Snapshot approach**: silent, unbounded drift is possible if nobody remembers to revisit a
  known-temporary fix. `scripts/rebuild_annotations.py`'s `PENDING_UPSTREAM_FIXES` (pinning issues #18/#19
  locally because their GitHub fields are still stale) is exactly this risk — it's a plain dict with a
  comment, not a tracked, queryable "still open" flag. Nothing forces it back into view once the upstream
  field is actually fixed; it just silently keeps overriding forever unless a human remembers to check.
- **Log approach**: the log format itself still has to evolve, and "never mutate, only append" doesn't
  make that free — old entries have to keep replaying correctly under newer replay code, or you snapshot
  and migrate, which quietly breaks the append-only purity claim. The earlier `Human`-interface design for
  raw zarr snapshots already anticipated this for its own metadata (`checkMetadata`: "additive-only
  structural diff against prior schema version") — schema evolution is a real cost an event log doesn't
  dodge, it just moves the problem from "diffing two full snapshots" to "keeping a replay function correct
  against every historical entry shape ever appended."

## Where this leaves it

Keep git-versioned snapshots. The deciding factor isn't tooling maturity or collaborator familiarity
(both real, both already argued in `schema.md`'s CUE discussion) — it's that this catalog's actual ground
truth lives outside the repo and is already cheaply re-askable, which is exactly the condition under which
event sourcing earns its keep the *least*. Two cheap changes get most of what an append-only log would
have offered, without adopting it:
1. Record real filesystem timestamps (`ctime`) per volume in `rebuild_volumes.py`'s output, instead of
   relying on "whenever this rebuild happened to run" as the only time signal.
2. If point-in-time annotation history is ever actually needed, query GitHub's own item timeline rather
   than build a parallel log — the authoritative history already exists there and `rebuild_annotations.py`
   is currently throwing it away by only reading the latest snapshot.

Revisit the whole question if the source of truth ever stops being externally re-derivable — e.g. if this
catalog started accepting facts nobody else records (a field with no GitHub Project or filesystem
equivalent, entered here first) — at that point this repo *would* become the authoritative record, and the
case for an append-only log gets substantially stronger.
